四级汇总词汇 · 07英文原文

The Last Page of the Diary

日记的最后一页 · 649 词 · 8 段 · 首次出现的目标词加粗

1A publisher asked Eva to edit her grandfather's diary. He had been a journalist, and a biographer had cited the first chapter in a biography. The diary was part of Eva's inheritance. A letter to her granddaughter asked the family to release it only with the last page. "Dear Eva" was still visible in her grandmother's careful writing. Eva expected a confession. She found a shopping list, a sketch of a broken clock, and a nickname. Curiosity overcame her reluctance to ask who it belonged to.

2The publisher wanted a paperback that read like a novel. Its proposed preface described the woman as an imaginary companion. Eva compared the diary with written correspondence in a local archive. A nonfiction account of the strike mentioned a night cleaner with the same nickname. A periodical printed her photograph at a funeral. The resemblance to the sketch was strong enough to interest Eva, but she still needed evidence of its authenticity. She asked an old reporter who had reviewed her grandfather's work to look at the page.

3He read the list and laughed at a witty note about bacon. Eva had taken it for a private joke. The reporter said workers often wrote food orders on the back of articles that editors rejected. He found a second page of prose with the same marks. Its opening paragraph contradicted her grandfather's published narrative. The cleaner had warned workers about a dangerous clock before an accident. The newspaper left that detail out. The reporter could cite the public edition, but he could only suppose why the editor omitted the warning.

4Her grandmother, now a widow, had grieved after a worker's death. She recalled her husband's shame, loneliness, and regret. He had felt ashamed of keeping his job and confused about what he owed the cleaner. Eva had mistaken a reminder in the journal for a romance. Her grandmother laughed at that imaginative guess, then began to cry. The writer had forgotten to give the woman credit. His last page tried to preserve a memory that could fade if nobody cared enough to narrate it.

5Eva requested a biographical note. Her grandmother agreed if the cleaner's perspective appeared in its own words. A literary critic found the document fascinating, but wanted an exhaustive introduction. An essayist offered scholarly commentary. Eva proposed a shorter, collaborative selection. A cartoonist could illustrate the broken clock, and the two accounts could make the contradiction plain. The drawing was thoughtful rather than provocative. A reader could see why a cleaner on the night shift knew something the newspaper's usual reviewer did not.

6A young reader thought the note too serious for a book that held poetry. She showed Eva a poem whose lyrics praised the workers. Their author had known the cleaner. An honest editor could keep that voice without calling it proof of the accident. Eva added an illustration and named both sources.

7The publisher feared that losing the supposed romance would disappoint eager readers. Eva let him recite two lines aloud. One praised the factory's punctuality. The other told the truth about its clock. The irony had more wit than the fictional chapter. A novelist read the proofs, checked the calendar, and said the correction was persuasive. They chose a small print edition and an ebook. It might never become a best-seller, but neither version would leave readers with a falsehood about the woman.

8At the launch Eva's niece held up the last page. A reviewer had written a voluminous description of the book and called the mystery compelling. The girl asked why the author would end it with a shopping list. Eva said the book was also about the cleaner's loss of credit. An essay on the woman's life appeared beside the sketch. Its quiet tone showed admiration for a person her family once forgot. The niece could now tell where the supposedly forgotten name came from.

四级汇总词汇 · 07中文译文

日记的最后一页

按英文段落顺序对照阅读

1一位出版商请伊娃编辑祖父的日记。祖父当过记者，一位传记作者引用过日记第一章。日记是伊娃继承的一部分。一封写给孙女的信要求家人出版时保留最后一页。祖母工整的笔迹里还能看出“亲爱的伊娃”。伊娃以为最后一页会有什么自白，翻开却看到一张购物清单、一只坏钟的草图和一个绰号。她忍不住想问，那个人究竟是谁。

2出版商希望做成一本读起来像小说的平装书。拟好的序言把那个女人说成想象中的伴侣。伊娃到地方档案馆，用往来信件对照日记。一份记录罢工的纪实材料提到同样绰号的夜班清洁工，一份期刊还刊过她参加葬礼的照片。照片和草图很像，伊娃仍需要证实记录是真的。她找来一位曾评过祖父作品的老记者。

3老记者读清单时，为一句拿培根打趣的话笑起来。伊娃原以为那是私人玩笑。老记者说，工人常把订餐单写在编辑退稿的背面。他找到有同样记号的另一页文章，开头就与祖父发表过的叙述矛盾。事故之前，清洁工曾提醒工人那只钟出了危险故障。报纸漏掉了这件事。记者能引出已刊的版本，编辑当初为什么删，只能推测。

4伊娃的祖母此时已经守寡。她回忆一个工人死亡后，丈夫既羞愧、孤单，又后悔。他觉得自己保住工作有些惭愧，不知道该怎样回报那名清洁工。伊娃还曾把日记里的提醒当成一场恋情。祖母听完这个想象先笑了，随后哭起来。写日记的人忘了公开给她记功，只能在最后一页保住一份可能随无人讲述而淡去的记忆。

5伊娃请祖母写一段人物说明。祖母答应，条件是清洁工的看法要用她自己的话呈现。一名文学评论家觉得材料很有意思，希望加上详尽导言。一位散文家愿意提供学术评论。伊娃提议一起挑出更短的材料。漫画家可以画出坏掉的钟，两份记载一对照，矛盾就清楚了。画面力求让人看懂，为什么夜班清洁工会知道平日报纸评论员不知道的事。

6一位年轻读者觉得，书里还有诗，说明却显得太严肃。她给伊娃看了一首赞扬工人的诗。诗的作者认识那位清洁工。诚实的编辑可以保留这种声音，同时避免把它当成事故证据。伊娃加了一幅插图，写明两种材料的来源。

7出版商怕删掉假想的恋情会让期待故事的人失望。伊娃让他大声念两行。一行夸工厂守时，另一行写那只钟的实情。这种反讽比小说章节更有意味。一位小说家读过校样，核对日历，觉得修订很有说服力。他们决定少量印刷，再做电子书。书也许不会畅销，但两个版本都不会给读者留下关于那名清洁工的错误说法。

8发布时，伊娃的侄女举起日记最后一页。一位评论者曾长篇介绍这本书，称谜团很吸引人。女孩问，作者为什么用购物清单结尾。伊娃说，书还写了那位清洁工没有得到应有的承认。草图旁是一篇介绍她生平的短文，语气平实，表达了对一位曾被家人遗忘的人物的敬意。女孩现在知道那个据说已经没人记得的名字从哪儿来了。
